utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, to continue your cross-examination. And we want to move as quickly as possible. The Chamber will be considering the whole question of time, use of time in relation to this case, and we'll be saying something about that shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've already made my position clear on this witness and generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Nice: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, as foreign minister for five years and permanent representative at the United Nations, my suggestion to you is you know full well the responsibility that this accused has for events that happened in Croatia and in Bosnia but that you haven't told us the full truth. Do you understand? It's my suggestion to you.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying, but at the same time, I would like to say that your claim is all wrong. Mr. Milosevic had very limited abilities to influence the development of events, both in Croatia and in Bosnia, and a number of facts I mentioned point in that direction. One of the facts being that he was among the first to insist that peace forces be brought to Croatia. He also accepted immediately all five peace proposals, and he was the key figure in the acceptance of the Dayton Peace Accords.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I move on to matters of substance I suggest that you've completely misled us in your observations about the desire to have all Serbs living in one area eventually, and that it is as clear as can be from all the documents that I've provided to you - and we'll look at a few of them, but not very many - it was as clear as can be that that was the underlying objective of everyone on both sides of the Drina. Correct or incorrect?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, that's incorrect. What is correct is that the Serbs across the Drina River, both in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia, insisted upon their constitutional right to self-determination, which was equal for all constituent nations in Yugoslavia. That constituent right of theirs was guaranteed both by the constitutions of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Exercising that right did not mean that they just wanted to annex their state to Serbia but that they had a choice to remain in the state that existed until that time. We supported their right just as we supported the rights that were available to other peoples living in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in Croatia and in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your suggestion, finally, of the matters I'm going to pick out, your suggestion that you didn't know of the level of support given by Serbia for the Krajina and also for the Serbs in Bosnia is simply absurd, I will suggest to you. A person in your position had to know the percentage and part of Serbia's income going to these interests, and you haven't told us the truth about that.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you are drawing conclusions too quickly, and those conclusions go against the facts. Let me reiterate that, in addition to supporting the rights of the Serbs across the Drina, both in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina, their right to self-determination, we supported them financially and materially in order to ensure their continued existence. We never concealed that fact. And it is true that certain financial means of Yugoslavia were sent to those former republics so as to ensure that those people would not starve to death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of what Mladic said at the 50th session of the RS Assembly in April 1995 about the percentage of support that he'd received over the previous years from Belgrade? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of what the accused himself said when he was arrested about the support he had provided for weapons and ammunitions and other needs of the army of the Republika Srpska constituting a state secret? That's what he said and was made publicly known. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the statement given by Mr. Milosevic when he was in prison in Belgrade, the statement relating to the financial assistance given to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... did that come as a complete surprise to you, foreign minister for five years, permanent representative for five years, and were you at one stage also a Deputy Prime Minister?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me it was quite a surprise, because I knew that we provided material support, but I didn't know about the details. I wasn't involved in any other discussions regarding that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... direct evidence here from Mr. Babic about direct funding provided at his request to this accused. Were you entirely unaware of that? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said to you that I was not involved in any discussions concerning military support and military issues. I didn't know any details about the material support that was provided to Serbs across the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My suggestion to you is that it's simply unacceptable and unrealistic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, just a matter of the record. Direct funding provided to this accused was provided by this accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My suggestion to you is your answer is simply and completely unrealistic. Let me remind you of a few facts: In the course of your duties, Serbia had four different Prime Ministers, the federal republic had three different Prime Ministers, there were four other foreign ministers, just to name some of the office holders. So as people were turning over, you remained a constant figure. Now, if things were being kept from government ministers and representatives at the UN, who was doing it; one of these other Prime Ministers, one of these other foreign ministers? Who was doing it? Who was keeping it from you?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what they had to keep from me, but in every government there is a division of tasks, and every minister is in charge of his responsibilities. Within my domain, I had to deal with the disintegration of Yugoslavia. I had to protect the reputation of the name of Yugoslavia in the world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... anyone, can you, who would have kept this information from you?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have an impression that anything is being concealed from me. I did not have much time --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you're telling us is that everything that was done was correct and above board and proper for one state to do in respect of the affairs of neighbouring territories, therefore, there would be no need to keep anything from you.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already stated what I know, and what I know is not something that Yugoslavia or Serbia can be blamed for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. The truth, Mr. Jovanovic, is this: That this accused, who didn't have a platform of his own, or a philosophy, rose to power in answer to the needs of others, the Serb intellectuals and probably also the Kosovo Serbs. True or false in your analysis?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not true, because you're neglecting the fact that the Serb people to a great extent were dissatisfied with the status they had within the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. It was constantly kept under control by the leadership of Croatia and Slovenia, and Josip Broz Tito constantly put in offices people who were obedient to him. Therefore, the Serbian people felt oppressed, and it is not a great surprise that Mr. Milosevic in the first free elections was elected by a great majority of votes as the first Serbian President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And once in office, and you shared offices -- you shared office or you had office for a long period of time, once in office, those of you there realised that, to stay in office, the accused needed to serve the interests of the constituencies that had supported him; nationalists, Kosovo Serbs, and he did everything that was necessary to stay in office; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an opinion that originated from our former western republics which wanted to portray Mr. Milosevic as a Serb nationalist. To my knowledge, he was never a Serb nationalist because he acknowledged equal rights to all peoples living in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you all knew that he had to serve the interests of the nationalists to stay in office, and he did whatever was necessary in support of the Bosnian Serbs and the Croatian Serbs to achieve that end; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not correct. Entirely incorrect. You have absolutely accepted the thesis of the former secessionists, Tudjman and Kucan, who launched that thesis in order to conceal their own secession which could not have been recognised had there been not this attack against Serbian leadership in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Nort's assistance, very rapidly, tab 8 of the defendant's documents on the overhead projector, the report of 30th of May over which some time was spent. If we just look, please, at this. First of all put it on the overhead projector for ease of reference. Page 3. I beg your pardon. Page 2, please, Mr. Nort. The overhead projector, please, technical booth. And page 3, please, for the usher. Third page. Yes. This report which we looked at included references in paragraph 8 to General Nedeljko Boskovic having conducted discussions with Bosnia and Herzegovina Presidency, and the suggestion is that he was unable, I think, to control Mladic. In fact, Boskovic did succeed in controlling Mladic on one occasion and bragged about it, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible, but I'm telling you I was not kept abreast of these military developments at all. I learned this from the report to the Secretary-General of the UN.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 9. "Given the doubts that now exist about the ability of the authorities in Belgrade to influence General Mladic ..." Then a few lines down, just to remind the Court, "While it is my hope that the shelling of the city will not be resumed, it is also clear that the emergence of General Mladic and the forces under his command as independent actors apparently beyond the control of JNA..." And then over the page, please, Mr. Nort, to paragraph 13: "The anomalous position of General Mladic and the forces under his command, who are subject neither to the authority of Belgrade nor to that of the government of Bosnia ..." Now, at the time of this report the JNA was just on the process of disintegrating and the VRS was just in the process of being formed; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army of Republika Srpska, as I understood, based on this report and other sources, was created by the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina who were in the JNA forces and deployed to Bosnia and Herzegovina located in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the changeover or the change of forces from being JNA to becoming in large part VRS, this document reflects some uncertainty as to the ability of either the JNA, as it makes clear, or Belgrade itself to influence him, but it's only expressing uncertainty, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I understood it, the JNA had great difficulties in withdrawing from Bosnia and Herzegovina their formations which had soldiers from Serbia and Montenegro in it because those soldiers were --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... short, this document is expressing uncertainty about the ability at that stage, and that's all. And this is the changeover stage, expressing uncertainty about the ability to control Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, where in the document do the -- does the document cite that as the basis of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, paragraph 9 says "... doubts about the ability ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but your thesis is that this was due to the changeover and you need to have a factual basis for that in the document itself if you're putting it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's a question of time. Paragraph 5: "The bulk of the JNA personnel who were deployed in Bosnia-Herzegovina were citizens of that republic and were not therefore covered by the Belgrade authority's decision of 4 May to withdraw the JNA from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Most of them appear to have joined the army of the so-called 'Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.'" It goes on to deal with the statistics on all that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking the witness: It's right, isn't it, this was at the time of the establishment of that army, that new army, and the changeover of authority, and all that this document is expressing is doubts about the ability of the JNA or Belgrade to control him, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The doubts are no proof at all. Anybody can have doubts. The JNA did have great difficulties in ensuring that they withdrew their forces from Bosnia and Herzegovina safely. The army of Alija Izetbegovic obstructed them in that endeavour. There were many victims in Dobrovoljacka street and Tuzla and so on. Therefore, the withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia-Herzegovina was obstructed on purpose by Alija Izetbegovic in order to use it in their campaign against Serbia and Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... move on. You can just help us with this: We know, and we're going to look at it very briefly, that immediately following this report there was a further Resolution of the Security Council, effectively condemning that the Serbs -- Security Council Resolutions are based on the totality of information coming to various members who are party to the Resolutions; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Resolution you have in mind. There was a Resolution where that was condemned and withdrawal was requested, but there was also a report of the Secretary-General confirming that the units of the JNA had withdrawn from the barracks from which withdrawal was obstructed by Alija Izetbegovic. As far as I know, the Presidency, on the 5th of June, officially informed the last soldier of the JNA had withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... procedural one which you as a permanent representative know, Resolutions are made on the totality of information coming to those engaged in drafting and approving the Resolution; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that is correct or not. Rather, I know that based on that information, they adopted certain documents. I don't know whether that information was complete, whether they also took into account information coming from Belgrade and Yugoslavia in general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first of the three topics I said I would speak to you about, namely the authority of the accused, I have only time for one other question this morning, and it's this: You told us about the development of the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Serbia. Both those ministries, set up under the 1990 act, I think, were abolished in 1993 while the third ministry established, the Ministry for Serbs Overseas, continued in effect. The Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Foreign Ministry, were abolished in 1993 because by then the accused had sufficient and adequate control over the FRY as not to need such ministries for Serbia. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that they were abolished, but the explanation you provided is incorrect, because in the meantime, the former Yugoslavia was reconstituted and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was created. Therefore, one year was needed in order for the organs to establish mutual links and relations, and when that was done it was decided those two ministries should be abolished because there was no purpose in their further existence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You understand the Prosecution's position on this, don't you, Mr. Jovanovic: There was in fact never a need for a Foreign Ministry for the Republic of Serbia nor a need for a Ministry of Defence in a country that claims it has no army. Those ministries were set up for a practical and -- for a practical purpose in 1990, and by 1993 the accused could get everything he wanted through the FRY. That is the reality, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not the reality, because in 1990, or in the former Yugoslavia, the state was in a very difficult situation. We didn't know how things were going to develop. Therefore, that constitution in 1990, as a measure of precaution, decided to establish these two ministries, and the Ministry of Defence existed practically only on paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Third topic that I was going to discuss to you, the prevailing ambition of all of you to achieve a state where all the Serbs could live together. There is one existing telephone intercept transcript -- no, I beg your pardon. I'm looking at the wrong document. My mistake. Can you look at this document, please. It's a new document, it's been referred to before, it comes from a book of documents. It's the declaration concerning the conditions for recognition of new states. Dated the 16th of December. If the usher would be good enough to put the second page on -- there it is. 16th of December, 1991, where the European Community, and we can look at the foot of that page, inviting all Yugoslav republics to state by the 23rd of December whether they wish to be recognised as independent. Do you remember this declaration and indeed this document?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. And I replied to this declaration. I spoke about that on the first day I gave testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What this -- what this document did, what this invitation did was to render forever obsolete the Belgrade initiative which sought the inclusion of Bosnia because Bosnia was bound to accept the invitation and apply for independence. It heralded the new departure of the third Yugoslavia which itself failed in the following year and it gave rise to the inevitability of war if the accused and those he represented were to have their way; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your approach is entirely wrong. It is prejudicial and selective. You're basically supporting the policy of European Community secessionist republics. The European Community supported from the beginning the secessionist policy which led to all the problems that ensued later. The Belgrade initiative wanted to continue the struggle for preserving the former Yugoslavia in which everybody lived together in prosperity. If a -- if an appeal was sent to Macedonia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was done precisely in order to reconstitute the new state and to turn it into a stable state where everybody would be guaranteed equality. Unfortunately, this initiative was not successful because it was undermined from elsewhere and because these republics were encouraged to proceed with their secession. Previously, it had already been decided to inflict a deadly blow upon Yugoslavia and to render it obsolete with the stroke of a pen. This was a crime against humanity and peace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. May tab 5 be produced, please. You're saying, are you, that the -- no, never mind. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. May tab 5 be produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tab 8, please, next, from the Prosecution proposed exhibits. This, Mr. Jovanovic, is quite an extensive intercepted telephone conversation between yourself involving Karadzic and Koljevic. It's already been produced, you've had an opportunity to look at it, and I see I think you took the documents away with you over the weekend and I'm glad you did so. Can I just look at two passages, please, Mr. Nort. In the English version at page 5, and I'm afraid I haven't checked -- it's already an exhibit. I haven't checked the parallel for page 5. I don't know if -- it's my mistake for not having that in hand. At page 5 -- page 5 has you saying in your conversation with Karadzic the only thing that is not mentioned here -- you were talking at this time - this is February of 1992 - is the unchangedness of borders, but you have no borders yet established. Now, have you found that passage? It will be about page 6 or 7.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read this. I've read it over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see this on the transcript of the conversation. It's on page 3 of the Serbian text. The last line on page 3, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you got that on page 3? You've read this in any event over the weekend. This makes it quite clear, doesn't it, that you were determined there should be no changing of the then-borders created in Bosnia. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wouldn't be right. If you read the entire conversation, and you should look at it as a whole and not extract a sentence out of context, this had to do with the preparations for the delegation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, for negotiations with Ambassador Cutileiro in order to establish a cantonal Bosnia. Mr. Karadzic wanted to check some of his thoughts and clarify some concepts because he wasn't clear about some legal concepts. I said here something that's correct, and that is that Bosnia and Herzegovina were yet to be constituted as an independent state on the basis of a cantonal order, and this process was under way, and they were to negotiate and reach a joint conclusion. I did not say that there would be no change of borders with Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, what is before us is not what you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry if it isn't. That's my mistake for not checking. But in any event, Your Honours, because of the length of the document, because the witness has now read it and because I had to ask the interpretation of the document to be a matter for the Chamber in due course, and I put my case, if the usher would be good enough to put page 6 on it, it picks up at page 6 and goes on to page 7, the passage I'm referring to him. The only thing that is not mentioned here is unchangedness of the borders. "You have no borders yet established..." and it's that passage that follows that I was referring the witness to. But, Your Honour, may I finish with this document in this way:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The cantonal approach of this, which is the Cutileiro plan, also found at our tab 25, was appealing to you and to the Serb leadership because it did indeed have ethnic borders. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was acceptable for the entire Conference on Yugoslavia, and all the participants, including Mr. Izetbegovic. Later he withdrew from this position, and he was persuaded to do so by America.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My case on that particular -- or my proposition on that particular intercept in mind, can we look briefly at tab 25, an existing exhibit, Exhibit 810, and to remind you of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, does that last one have an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, it's an existing exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I certainly do. It is 613, tab 243.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again, it's a document we've looked at before but not with you, Mr. Jovanovic. It's a Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs document. You have seen it, you've gone through it over the weekend, I have no doubt, and without taking time on it, because it's available to the Court, the last paragraph that comes from your Ministry of Foreign Affairs, says this -- second page, please, Mr. Nort, last paragraph: "Value of the Cutileiro's Plan rested with that the International Community already at that time showed its readiness to legalise and verify internationally and legally the borders of Serbian territories in BiH." Now, these were ethnical borders and this was the value to you, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ethnical borders also exist in the Dayton Accord, and that has been accepted by the whole world. It was the only way to calm down Bosnia-Herzegovina and prevent it from rushing into war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm dealing with things chronologically, trying to enable the Court to have a chronological picture. This is the Cutileiro plan. You're writing about it after the event in 1994 but it's a 1992 event. And at that stage the attraction of this plan, and you've gone on about how you say every peace plan was accepted, the actual attraction of this plan was its ethnical borders which were going to be recognised internationally; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all the other plans the internal ethnic borders were recognised. This was an expression of the right to self-determination of the three constituent peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I see nothing bad or terrible about it. That's why it was accepted by the international community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next document is tab 12, which is the stenographic record of the Council for Harmonisation that met on the 11th of August. Just while it's coming up, to remind the Court, the Council for Harmonisation, wider than the SDC, with representations from the RS and the RSK. Again you will have gone through this over the weekend so we can deal with it all very swiftly, but at page 23 in the English --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice's question contains a substantive error. He can see that in the stenogram. This Council for Harmonisation was drawn up by members of the council established by the then president of Yugoslavia, Dobrica Cosic. The members of the council are listed, and it can clearly be seen that the representatives of the RS and the RSK were not members of that council, and they were invited by the chairman to participate. Therefore, there were no representatives outside the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in this council, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... cut into my time. I have no time to afford to give to the accused, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What he's saying is you have made a misrepresentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's wider than the SDC.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There was no representation from the RS and RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the composition is not the representation, he can deal with it in re-examination, but I'm grateful for the intervention and if I may deal with it in a question, it's in this way:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is for a council -- Perhaps Mr. Nort would put the first page of the document on the overhead projector, since the accused raises it. As translated this embodies the Council for Coordination of points of view on state policy. Incidentally, you can see it was actually held in Dobanovci. I asked you about that, you didn't recall it; never mind. Coordination of whose points of view, Mr. Jovanovic? Whose points of view were to be coordinated? If it wasn't the RS and the RSK who were invited along, whose points of view were to be coordinated?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The points of view of the federal organs and the organs of the republic were to be harmonised with the new president, Milan Panic, who frequently acted very independently without a thorough understanding of the problems and issues involved. In order to protect him from his embarking on facts which were not familiar to him, he was to be familiarised with these issues and conclusions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there to be coordination with those coming along, if not as representatives of the council nevertheless coming along on, I think, all the occasions we've looked at from the RS and the RSK, was there to be coordination with them? Was that what it was about?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These meetings were convened by the president of the Republic of Yugoslavia, Mr. Cosic, and with reference to the representatives of the Serbs from Bosnia and Herzegovina, they were only consultative. They were to be given advice or clarifications with respect to previous meetings; for example, the London conference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 23 in the English, please, and 23 at the bottom. I hope it's the same pagination as mine. It's not the same as mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I became alert yesterday to the fact that there was a marginal difference of pagination between my pages and -- can I have the document back? Thank you very much. No, top of page 23 it will be. Right. The top of page 23 -- top of page 23, please. Top. Right at the top. Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We see a passage - this is you speaking - and it says this: "However, I am really afraid that the other side, the opponents' side doesn't want that because it wants clear and clean discontinuity, that psychological second to set in. That's important for them because of their strategic aspirations for the Balkans and because they want to deny us the position of Piedmont, that is the possibility that tomorrow or in ten or fifty years we become a new centre which will bring Yugoslav peoples together." Pausing there, Piedmont is a reference to the province of Italy that occupied a broadly similar position to Serbia at the unification of Italy in the 19th century. It goes on: "That is something that the previous generations have put into our hands. We have no right to throw it away. We may choose not to use it at the time when conditions are unfavourable, but we should still preserve it, because if it were not so important, it would not brother our opponents so much." This, Mr. Jovanovic, is another clear announcement by you of the desirability of leaving the situation so that all Serbs could live in one state, and it was the underlining purpose and it was as plain as could be.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what was said. What was said was that all the southern Slavs have the right to a common state. This was their dream for centuries, and it was realised in 1918. Unfortunately, the European Community managed to turn it into dust and ashes. If Serbia was Piedmont for the southern Slavs, this a historical fact. This is why Austria-Hungary waged the First World War against Serbia, so as to prevent that. The shedding of large quantities of blood in these unfortunate wars was a pledge that nothing like that would happen again in the future. The noble desire of all the southern Slavs are something that no other southern Slav would give up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would the usher please bring me the papers and I'll just have a look for one other short passage from this document, because it may not be the same page number and I can just about afford the time to do it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that, probably from reading the transcript of this trial, that an issue is whether there was equality of approach to the Serbs in Bosnia and Croatia and the Serbs -- and the Kosovo Albanians. You know about that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. There was not and could not have been a single approach because these were constituent peoples, and this was guaranteed by the constitutions of these peoples in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Albanians in Kosovo were an ethnic minority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... let's look at this passage where the accused is speaking in the same meeting. He recognised full well - top of the page, please. That's fine. He recognised, we can see it at the top of the page, the validity or the problem of that argument, because he says this: "I didn't have any reservations with regards to this, but an explanation how to avoid with what arguments that the same right is requested for the Albanians, that is the problem. This is the thorn in our argumentation. We know what our arguments are, we have to see what arguments will be acceptable to them." The inconsistency of approach between Serbs and Kosovo Albanians was always recognised, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In this case, as far as I understand, Mr. Milosevic pointed out that we have a constitution which differentiates between minorities and constituent peoples. However, the international community, or rather, its western part, did not recognise this distinction. It also forcibly demoted the Serbs in Bosnia and in Croatia to the status of minorities. This led to conflicts and ultimately it was recognised that the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina are a constituent people. This was not the case in Croatia where they were reduced to the status of a minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next exhibit, please, is tab 15, which is the shorthand notes for the meeting on the 9th of January. I've got a few rather more references to look at in this one but the page numbering won't be a problem. If the page -- if the usher could have the English, and it's page 25 at the bottom -- beg your pardon, it's page -- page 25, at the bottom of the page. Usher, that's the big page 25, in the middle, not the page on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is Dobrica -- this is yourself speaking, and it's at the top of the page, Usher, please. Thank you. Top of the page. No, next page, please. It's 25 at the bottom. It's the big page number 25. This is you speaking, and you said this: "We have to make a conclusion from it that the community and conditions do not allow the ages old dream on union of all Serbs in one Serbian country to become true. We have to move in phases towards that goal." Mr. Jovanovic, it couldn't be clearer from all the passages I'm putting to you that this was your underlying intention and it was shared by everyone else. "Move in phases towards that goal." Tell me what that means.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your conclusion is not correct. What I said here and repeated later on was that all the Serbs did live in one state, Yugoslavia, and they were expelled from it against their will. The discussion now was about their wish to remain in one state, and I told them that this was no longer realistic and possible. In one of the texts you put to me, I said expressly that the right to self-determination of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina does not include the right to secession --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... next is page 43 of --

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the standpoint I put forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Bottom right-hand corner, page 43 of 1167. And middle of the page, of that page. Not that one. It's page 43 of 1167. Further on. No. Page -- sorry. If you look at the bottom right-hand corner, Mr. Nort, you'll see figures 43. Bottom right-hand corner, please. Your Honours will know that these pages have been helpfully compiled so that one can cross refer to the Serbian, but that makes it more difficult for Mr. Nort and I'm sorry about that. No. Page 43 at the bottom right-hand corner, please. Can I have the papers back?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the accused speaking in this meeting. Couldn't be clearer: "The name of the state is not important," he said, "the essence is important. What matters here is that the ethnical division is fully accepted and that the constitutive people is accepted. These are the two elements that Alija tried to avoid by all means. There could be no unitary state with these two elements." Now, this is dealing with the division of Bosnia along ethnical division, and it was ethnical division that was uppermost in the accused's mind; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is about the Vance-Owen Plan that the Serbs in Bosnia accepted in principle but they rejected the maps. Mr. Milosevic made an effort to convince them to accept the maps to which they had numerous objections. This was a way of having them accept a rational way of thinking and accept the maps --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- it was not a plea for ethnic purity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... bottom right-hand corner. The same figures we've been looking at. Mr. Jovanovic, in my respectful submission, you are denying what is absolutely obvious and you're doing it because you know that this lay behind the support of the Bosnian Serbs and it lay behind the crimes that were committed. And if you look at this, this is Dobrica Cosic talking. Further up the page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, let him answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Mr. Nice, that you are getting involved in your own expectations about the outcome and coming into conflict with the facts. Before the declaration and after that we kept stressing that we had no territorial pretensions, that all we wanted was the freedom and equality of the Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's the reason Mr. Milosevic immediately accepted the Cutileiro plan. He said that two or three weeks after that he would recognise Bosnia and Herzegovina. Why was this not done? Why was this plan toppled and Bosnia and Herzegovina led into war?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look at this passage from Dobrica Cosic presiding over the meeting: "In my opinion, we have to reconcile ourselves and finally agree that the achievement of our main political goal, living in one state or in the federation of states, is the long-term aim which could be achieved only step-by-step or gradually. I think that any other kind of a national and state politics would be an adventure." What does that mean if it doesn't mean what I'm suggesting?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means quieting the frustrated leaders of the Bosnian Serbs who were afraid of their own shadows. They were afraid of being tricked by Alija Izetbegovic, and they persistently refused to accept the maps. Both President Cosic and President Milosevic tried to calm their fears and to convince them that what they would gain would guarantee their freedom and equality. This is the rhetoric they used which was not foreign to any real southern Slav because we used to live in a single state and we are all nostalgic and wish that state had continued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's see what the accused said about this. Two pages on, please, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. Nort, at page 73, starting at the top of the page, a passage we've looked at before. And Mr. Jovanovic, you will have looked at this. This is the passage where the accused says, and it's at the top of the page: "How can we --" five lines down -- "how to turn the situation which de facto exists --" no, top of the page, please. Yep. Five lines down. "How to turn the situation which de facto exists and which could not be de facto endangered into being de facto and de jure," and he deals with the small labyrinth and says how long it will take to get there. There had been achieved by force what it was now the desire of the accused to turn, by passage of time, by negotiations, into law; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All this is part of the methodology of quieting the fears of the leaders of the Bosnian Serbs and convincing them to accept the maps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I haven't got time to go into it but let's go over four pages to page 76.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a passage I would press the Chamber to read in great detail at some stage, but at page 76, at the bottom right-hand corner, middle of that page, where we see about something called cutting the boat loose. That relates to -- in fact, let's pick it up at the top of the page, please, Usher. Radovan Karadzic deals with, first of all, the assassination the previous day of the Deputy Prime Minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina, saying that they'd punish the man. They never did. It's right, isn't it, they never punished the man who -- Karadzic never punished the man who assassinated Irfan Turalic [phoen], did he? As a matter of fact --

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Every murderer has to be tried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We go on, on a new topic, and Karadzic says: "We would act the way we agree, especially if we would be in a situation to endanger the position of the mother country ... We would 'cut our boat loose' ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "We're not speaking about 'cutting the boat loose.'" Cosic: "Who could sacrifice you? Who is entitled to make a decision to sacrifice the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina?" Karadzic: "I would like to say we are deluding ourselves by thinking that in a later phase we would be able to trick them." The accused: "They would already be tricked after we get the issue to the later phase. We have already 'led them up to the garden path.' That is the matter." Had they been led up the garden path, please? How had they been led up the garden path, Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, this entire text has to be read in its entirety to understand the real meaning of this. The entirety says that the Bosnian leaders, the Serb Bosnian leaders were so terrified that they kept saying things that were not rational, and at this meeting everyone, especially Presidents Cosic and Milosevic, took a great deal of trouble to get them to see reason. If they used words to pacify them, it was only in order to get them to accept the maps. That was the only meaning of all this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who had been led up the garden path?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I know from which page Mr. Nice is quoting? I can't find the passage, or perhaps I misheard the page number. He said page 76.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 76 in the English, and in the Serbian it's page 71.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the people who were led up the garden path were the international community, weren't they, Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't find it in Serbian, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... page 72 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not on page 71.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: End of page 72.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you have it in front of you, Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the English text in front of me. However, the page is not marked in the English version. I have it somewhere here too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't find this expression, to trick.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you, in Serbian it says that I said that we have already been able to deal with them. I didn't say to trick. I said to deal with them, to better them. This is a substantial difference, because I'm referring to tactics here and to persuasion, as Mr. Jovanovic has explained. To deal with somebody and to trick somebody are two different things.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then Karadzic says: "Had we realised this on time, then this border -- or we would have been in a different situation. And I responded with a joke, saying this is as though Pero had gone to the police. And only somebody who understands the language truly can understand what this is all about. This is just all excerpted from the context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can we have the Serbian put on the ELMO so we can have it translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour just give me one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice may at a later stage have occasion to ask you about this, Mr. Milosevic, depending on the course you take.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I said at a later stage in the proceedings you may have an opportunity to put that question to Mr. Milosevic himself, depending on the course he takes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Here it is. On the overhead projector, please, Mr. Nort. Bottom of the page. And if the interpreters please could read out the answer starting the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slobodan Milosevic: "We have beat them at their game. We have outwitted them if we put the matters to a later phase. What we have here is that we have managed to outwit them. This is what this is all about."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I must move on. The time is so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- short. If I could have that page back, please, Usher. I'm going to abandoned the rest of my questions on this topic and I'm going to move to the second topic -- I'm going to go to the second topic, crimes and knowledge of crimes. Tab 3, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, in that -- I'm sorry to go back to that passage. There was nothing in it about leading them up the garden path, from the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, not from the translation. The outwitted. If we put the matter, I think it's outwitted them. I'll try and get some detail of the translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is a very poor translation then, because that has a specific connotation in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll try to deal with that in more detail later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tab 3 is an existing intercept. You've had a chance to look at this, have you, over the weekend, Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we look at the English, please, on Exhibit 613, tab 101. Two things, remind the Chamber. If the usher would put page 4, looking at the bottom, on the overhead projector. We see a discussion between Karadzic and the accused about the London agreement triggered by discussion with the previous witness, Smilja Avramov.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you involved in any discussions about going back to the London agreement of 1915 which would have given Serbia so much more territory?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that I attended that meeting, if my memory serves me right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... please, Mr. Nort. You're aware of the London agreement and the maps that were discussed in London in 1915, are you?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you accept the view that another witness called by the accused has given that to discuss the London agreement maps would constitute embracing the notion of Greater Serbia? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, that was not the notion of Greater Serbia. Rather, an offer of Western allies extended to the Serbs during the war, namely to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... next question was to discuss those maps. Would it be right that to discuss those maps would be to embrace the notion of a Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes. Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say, Mr. Robinson, that this is way too much. Mr. Nice is putting questions as though I discussed the London agreement here, although he can see clearly for himself that I -- that Karadzic said that the meeting ought to be prepared --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let Mr. Nice -- put the question again, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on, Your Honour, if I may. It's dealt with already in other evidence and another intercept. Page 5, please, Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The accused here deals with --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is being done in a wrong way, Mr. Robinson. This is a manipulative way. Mr. Nice --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... manipulative -- if it is manipulative, we will deal with that. We haven't found it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the accused speaking, on page 5, halfway down. Karadzic says: "The problem are these idiots." And then expletive. "I see now they are bringing the Presidency into question." The accused says: "If they start that, then disturbances will start down there and they will be gone. We have to likewise secure Herzegovina down there up to Dubrovnik. That's what we should go for. The de facto situation in Yugoslavia is defending its territory." That's a contemporaneous 26th of October, 1991, intercept. You were foreign minister at the time. What you were doing in Dubrovnik, attacking it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is probably not an error of Mr. Nice but an error made by somebody who prepared this, because everything is turned upside down here. Where it should be Karadzic, it says Milosevic, and vice versa. So this is one great confusion. It says here Slobodan Milosevic says: "Very well, President, we will certainly get --" and then the person speaks in Ekavian and that's not the dialect I use, and I certainly wouldn't address Karadzic as Mr. President. So this is attributed to the wrong person. What Mr. Karadzic -- what Mr. Nice is reading out are not words uttered by me. So this is turned upside down, and does not reflect the conversation at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, are you saying that the passage attributed to you, which reads in English, "Yes, if they start that then disturbances will start down there and they will be gone," et cetera, that's not something that you said?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely what I'm saying. This is reflected in a different way in Serbian language, and this is something I didn't utter either. "Yes, and if we do that, then unrest will break out down there. However, we also have to deal with Herzegovina, whereas --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- "Dubrovnik --" and then another word in the Ekavian. So these are not my words. This has been put upside down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We understand the point. Mr. Nice, if that is so, then I don't see how you can work on this basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the swapping of names has been dealt with in the report of Mrs. Tromp. It's before you in the report. I'll deal with it after the break so I can explain exactly but my understanding is that these words are the accused's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The words that I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, the words --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- quoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The words -- it doesn't matter. Just for the avoidance of any doubt, Mr. Jovanovic -- even if they're not his words he's being seized of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think we need clarification of all this. We're trying to trace the exhibits and how this arose. We think this is an exhibit that came in through Mr. Lilic, and reference we have in the Prosecution exhibit witness list doesn't seem to tie up with the tab that we've got in the Prosecution schedule here. There's plainly an issue over the translation, as the Court will see the question mark next to the reported speech. So whoever translated it had an issue as to who was the appropriate speaker. If my memory serves me correct, Mrs. Tromp was not a witness in the case, in the end, and so any report by her on this issue is an internal matter for Mr. Nice, but in terms of exhibits in the case, I don't think there is any explanation about this and it is an issue that has not been resolved. We're concerned that there seem to be material inaccuracies. I don't know who has translated this document, where it originates from, and whether it has been checked by the translation department in this building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which tab number is it, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's 469, tab 40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On the Prosecution's --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Oh, right. I've got a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's 613 then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Oh, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I come back to that, because the time that's being taken will take me over the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is tab 3. This is tab 3, which I received within this binder from Mr. Nice. However, please take a look at this. Let me just prove to you that everything has been put upside down. On page 1, it says as though Karadzic said to me, "Tomorrow, here -" meaning in Belgrade - "in Sava centre, there is a large gathering of Montenegrins." And then I reply to that, "Is it really?" as though I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Put the page 1 on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Wait, Mr. Milosevic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to compare that to what comes later. It says here, "Here in Sava centre there is a large gathering of Montenegrins." And then Slobodan Milosevic says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. We'll deal with it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice will not put any more questions on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- put any more questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: On the basis of that tab. We'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 4, please. Tab 4 is a new exhibit. It's another of The Hague document exhibits of the kind introduced by the accused when leading this witness. If the usher would lay -- the Chamber therefore has it in its own papers. It's dated the 15th of November of 1991. And if the usher would take us to the third page now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us that there was nothing going on in Dubrovnik. When pressed in November of 1991, Mr. Jovanovic, "both Mr. Milosevic and Foreign Minister Jovanovic stressed that Serbia was not involved in the siege of Dubrovnik in any way. They did, however, defend JNA actions there, claiming that the JNA would deblock Dubrovnik only when mercenaries sheltering there in violation of a 1955 declaration," and so on, had been withdrawn. What was the action of the JNA, please, that you were defending? Was it the attack on Dubrovnik Old Town?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The JNA -- I cannot say that the JNA was at sea and remained there in order to block the city. I suppose that Croatian units were on the ramparts and were shooting from there at the valley belonging to the Serbs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... that. What's your evidence for that?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But they were -- Dubrovnik was declared to be under UNESCO's protection and no armed forces were allowed to be deployed in that city. As far as I know, that was violated and the JNA said that it would deblock the city once Croatia abided by the status of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What JNA action were you defending, Mr. Jovanovic? That's what I want to know. Because you know that by this time the evidence shows that Dubrovnik had been attacked by the JNA. Now, tell us, what were you defending?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not defend the attack on Dubrovnik. To the contrary. In one of the interviews given to Spiegel, I stated that we did not have any claims to any cities on Croatian coast, including Dubrovnik and any other city. What this refers to is that the status of Dubrovnik was abused and there were armed units there endangering Serbs' positions in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the JNA was at sea and said that it would deblock the city once Croatia withdrew its forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell us, as the foreign minister, did you then or have you at any time since come to appreciate that Dubrovnik was attacked by the JNA as indeed two trials in this very court have covered? Were you aware of that, Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, I learned --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- including from the trial ---

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you learn about it?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned first at the conference in The Hague, when President Tudjman complained that there had been attacks on Dubrovnik that was denied by the then-representative of the JNA. That's all I knew at the time. There was a claim and a denial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, I learned something more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I must take the most interesting question I can. Can you help the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Judges, please, looking back, with how it could conceivably be that you, the foreign minister, with such a world famous problem as the alleged attack on Dubrovnik, covered by the world's press, can have been unaware of the fact that the JNA was attacking it? Just explain what happened in government that you could have been kept out of knowledge.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time in Croatia there was a conflict between Croatian forces and the JNA. Croatian forces blocked the JNA barracks, and it was difficult to ensure that they were deblocked without casualties. There were -- there were a number of hot spots in the entire territory of Croatia. Dubrovnik was one of them. We were waiting for a peaceful resolution. We worked on a peaceful resolution. I never followed the developments in Dubrovnik closely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, the question is a fairly simple one. It is: How could Dubrovnik be attacked by the JNA and you as the foreign minister would not have been aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew as much as everybody else in Yugoslavia knew. I did not ever receive any special information about what was happening there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic -- if His Honour is finished?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- I am going to make it quite clear to you that my suggestion to you is that that answer by you is absolutely ridiculous. To say that you, the foreign minister, one of the only long-time serving associates of this accused for a ten-year period, because this is admittedly at an early part, a trusted associate of this accused, it is ridiculous for you to say you had no more knowledge of the JNA attack on Dubrovnik than the members of the public, and it reflects your need on behalf of this accused to deny the obvious.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is your conclusion, Mr. Nice. It may sound absurd, but it is true. I've sworn to say only the truth here, and that's what I did. Now, as to how logical and acceptable it is to somebody else, that's another matter, but this is truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at tab 12 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Jovanovic, then can I ask this way: When did you come to know that Dubrovnik was attacked and shelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say that accurately, but I think it was the first time here, at the conference in The Hague when President Tudjman complained. He was quite angry and spoke in an agitated way. I think that General Kadijevic was there as well, if my memory serves me right. He denied that, and he linked it to the blocking of the barracks throughout Croatia. He asked that that action be ceased and the JNA units be allowed to withdraw in peace without harassment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you did after you heard the news of shelling Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was nothing else I could do. I simply heard the explanation given by the JNA representative. We never discussed that matter. For me, Dubrovnik was an unknown, although that looks perhaps illogical. I never understood why Dubrovnik would be attacked, therefore, I never justified that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we look briefly at tab 12, the shorthand notes for the Council of Coordination of Points of View on State Policy of the 11th of August, at page 12 on the bottom right-hand corner, Usher, middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: See now this -- that's fine, thank you very much. This is one that you attended in August 1992 with, amongst others, Milo Djukanovic, who was at that time, oscillating as he does between president and Prime Minister, Prime Minister of the Republic of Montenegro, and this is what he had to say, in the middle of the page. You see it at the top of the screen: "I think that we should start from the judgement, if you agree, which has also its continuation in comparison with the judgement given by Mr. Panic, our federal Prime Minister. It is true that we did a lot of bad things during the previous period; a bad picture was created ..." What were the bad things that Mr. Djukanovic of Montenegro was talking about? Because you know that Montenegro was involved in the attacks on that part of Croatia, don't you? What was he talking about? What were these bad things?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably volunteers from Montenegro who went there and behaved rather badly, if I can say so, in moderate terms, and that probably embittered him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having access to all the top brass of the army, to the presidents and Prime Minister of Montenegro, to this accused, and with the world outcry amongst -- about, amongst other things, Dubrovnik, did you ever ask anybody if they'd attacked Dubrovnik or did you just not bother?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked and was told that we did not attack and that Serbia had nothing to do with that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that was a conflict --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you ask?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked President Milosevic, among others, and was given a clear answer that Serbia had nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was any explanation given for how the world could have been looking at the videos it was on television and seeing these attacks? Was any explanation given for that? Who was it said was firing the guns?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't go into details. What I know and what was discussed is that the Croats themselves in Dubrovnik, that's what was said and was written, set tyres on fire and that produced a lot of smoke and the international TV crews declared that to be explosions of shells fired by the JNA. I did not go into details, but this is what was presented in the press.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Somebody else's fault and the Serbs entirely innocent again; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. I simply said about what I had heard and read in the press. I couldn't take it for granted, but I had no other reliable information from other sources and therefore I awaited the day when the full truth would come out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, could you remind me, please, were you at that time foreign minister of Yugoslavia or of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this was in October of 1991 - I think that's what we said - then I was the minister of Serbia, until July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tab 13, please, the meeting on the 18th of August, 1992. At the bottom, right-hand corner it will be page 18. Now, here we see Milan Panic speaking. He had yet to be dismissed or removed by the accused. Milan Panic: "We are already in that position. The problem is that we've been accused for the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that we support the war in Bosnia, and that we left weapons for them to fight; that we support Karadzic financially. We spoke here about the ethnic cleansing." Now, the first thing is everybody understood, didn't they, Mr. Jovanovic, the allegations being made against Serbia and the FRY by the international community; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Panic simply conveyed what was said by the part of the international community against Serbia. These are not his claims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I accept that. Now let's look at the bottom of the page, please. Having set out the general allegations, he says: "We cannot get rid of it. This afternoon I received the following information - ethnic cleansing has begun: 15.000 Muslims from Sanski Most were given eight hours to leave their homes and make twenty kilometres to Jajce in order to reach the Muslims. This information was received from the United Nations. They asked me and said that I should stop it." You told us a couple of days ago that you reacted against any suggestions of and condemned any ethnic cleansing. Where are we going to find - help us, please - the public condemnation of the ethnic cleansing of Sanski Most by this body or by its leaders?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say with certainty whether we spoke about this, but the republican government and the federal government in their declarations, statements, frequently condemned ethnic cleansing, urged that there be a cease-fire and that all camps be disbanded if they existed. I don't know whether Sanski Most was mentioned specifically, but in this text and in other texts we saw here, we could see that I always condemned ethnic cleansing and insisted that humanitarian efforts be stepped up, that all camps be disbanded, that there be a cease-fire and end of hostilities, and we appealed to the other side to do the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My suggestion to you is that when the Chamber looks at this record of the meeting as a whole, and you were there, you will not find surprise, shock, and revulsion at the ethnic cleansing but tolerance of it.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on our side, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I hope to finish. I've got a few more things to deal with and I must complete the exercise that took a lot of time on the last occasion of producing the notice documents which are extremely important, not least because they cover the period of the aftermath of Srebrenica. I will ask the accused again, through the Court, whether the balance of those documents which the witness will have had an opportunity to consider simply be admitted en masse. I understand I didn't ask for tab 4 to be admitted and should have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted. We will take the break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, two matters to tidy up. First of all, the intercept transcript at tab 3. The accused is correct. At that particular point, the names should be reversed. In fact, it was covered in -- there's no reason for anybody to know this: It was covered in an electronic filing and a filing, an electronic filing that came to the Court on the 19th of January, 2004, where the particular point the transcript having speakers reversed towards the end was made, and I think the particular speakers were also reversed. So my error to have read it out the way I did. My point would remain the same, whether the knowledge -- or substantially the same, whether the knowledge going to the accused or going from him. The second point to deal with is the challenged translation, of course coming from the CLSS, that led to the phrase "up the garden path." The phrase that was actually used and is, in inverted commas, I believe translates to the effect of saying you take someone across the water and he remains thirsty on the other side. And it may be that it is itself a strong phrase, along the lines of leading up the garden path. So that's that. If I can now turn back to the questions of this witness and go back in time for one purpose only, because I should have -- although I've admitted many things, there's one thing I have to deal with just to put it in context. If we could go to tab 11, please, which is an existing exhibit, just simply to remind the Trial Chamber of the chronology of events when it was concerned about tab 8 of the accused's bundle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, Mr. Jovanovic, that this exhibit, tab 11, which you will have had a chance to review -- I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't have it before me right now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The usher will put it on the overhead projector. This is the Security Council Resolution that was made on the day of the report that you've been referring to, and we can see that it reaffirms its Resolutions, it reaffirms its support for the Conference on Yugoslavia. It deplores the fact that the demands have not been complied with, and it goes on to make the recommendations that it does. This led to sanctions. And as I suggested to you earlier on, the reality is that those making this Resolution would be relying on a whole range of sources of information, including the report had it, you say, not been delayed in its delivery, but they in fact have a whole range of information to rely on before making their Resolution; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it is based on, but the report that was delayed in arriving as the Resolution had already been adopted was the basis for this Resolution. Had the report arrived, the Resolution would not have been adopted and sanctions would certainly not have been introduced against Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is a matter of conjecture, I suggest to you. You suggested to the Chamber that somebody intentionally kept it back. Do you want to name that person for me, please, so I can investigate it?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I read, this was some Austrian clerk. I don't know what his name was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So an Austrian -- on your understanding, an Austrian clerk took the initiative to hold back a report for political reasons. Is that what you're suggesting? And may we have his name, if you want to make allegations like this.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what his name is, but the press said it was some sort of Austrian clerk or official.
