Whether he did this on his own initiative or pursuant to a suggestion from someone, I can't say. As all this is very unclear, all I can say is that the delay in the report's arrival was intentional.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The press in what country, Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Austria. An Austrian official.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no. I asked -- you said the press said that it was an Austrian official, and I was asking the press from what country made that allegation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found this in the Yugoslav press, but they were relying to sources from the foreign press. I don't know what sources. It's a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Jovanovic, the report is completely out of line with all the other Resolutions and reports, I must suggest to you, and of course it's possible sometimes for the Yugoslav interest to persuade some reporting person from an embassy here or there to take a different view, but the vast majority of the reporting was all to the same effect over this period, wasn't it? And that's why the various Resolutions were made.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question quite well. Generally speaking, yes, but this Resolution depended to a great extent on this report. And had the report been submitted, the sanctions would not have been introduced, at least not at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tab 16, please, which is the council meeting for the 21st of January of 1993. And if the usher would take us straight away to page 30, bottom right-hand corner. Apparently it's the same in the B/C/S. Here we're looking at something that Zivota Panic said. So no doubt about his military authority, could there be -- his knowledge of military matters, could there be, Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at that time he was the Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see what he had to say. "Next: What should now be done in Bosnia and Herzegovina? As far as I can estimate, Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina are losing both the territory and certain important facilities. We should agree here what is to be done regarding this issue. Things happening on the left bank of the Drina River, around Srebrenica, Bajina Basta, Bratunac, et cetera, are very bad, and you should know, Mr. President, that this is a disgrace for the Serbian people. They are running away, leaving everything. The help we are giving in weapons, ammunition, is located in some houses in villages. We could not pull it out. We are preparing to destroy it." How about that?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this a question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Leaving weapons behind for the Serbs, were you?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what General Panic said, as can be seen from the text. This is what he knew. I did not have this knowledge. I had the opportunity of hearing it at that time meeting. The meeting was an exchange of opinions about this topic, the topic of preparations for the London conference, if I remember correctly, and different views were expressed. Everyone expressed their own views. He was providing a military view of the situation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, what are you saying?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't find this. On page 30, somebody else is speaking. It has nothing to do with Panic. And then later on I can see Panic speaking but I can't find the words quoted by Mr. Nice. What page is this, please? I've found it now. I do apologise. It's page 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the end of this page we also see this, if the usher would move the page up a little bit: "People are leaving the territory on the left bank of the Drina River. They are leaving everything and running away. The map most probably caused this. They saw that this was not their territory and wanted to leave the area as soon as possible. That should be explained to them. "I think that somebody should come to Mt. Tara on Saturday. I will go and arrange what we should do and how. We must not lose control over that territory." Mount Tara guards the Drina from the east. This is your general saying "We must not lose that territory," territory in another state. Why was he saying that without your objecting to it? You as the foreign secretary, you should be objecting, saying you can't interfere in somebody else's business. Why didn't you object, Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I think that General Panic was referring to the Serbs in Bosnia, that they were not keeping this under control. Secondly, I did keep saying at that meeting that all hostilities were to cease, that there should be no ethnic cleansing, that refugees should return, and that self-determination did not mean secession. I kept repeating our political standpoint, that we had no pretensions on the territory of the neighbouring republic but that we would support the Serbs in Bosnia in claiming equal rights to the other two ethnic groups in Bosnia. What the general had in mind was that the Serbs in Bosnia were not controlling this territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 34, please. And I'll try and find it for the accused. Page 34, middle of the page, the accused speaking. I think it's probably on the accused's page 39, I think. And we just see this sentence halfway down the page: "It suits us very much that they have accepted the principle of demarcation according to the ethnic criteria. We should not 'befog' that principle a lot with some big story on economy ..." And then the matter goes back to the point that they would create some political mixers which would mix all that. The accused's pre-concern or preoccupation Mr. Jovanovic, just Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. like everybody else's, was to keep ethnic demarcation lines in order to lay the plan for ultimate union of Serb territory. Isn't this obvious from all these meetings?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conclusion is not only not obvious, it's not correct. At the same meeting, I recommended to the Serbs in Bosnia that they should not pay a great deal of attention to the national issue but the economic issue. If they could not survive economically, they would all want to join third countries in order to survive. This is only confirmation. The international representatives had already offered maps divided along ethnic lines. If this was acceptable to the international community, why should it not be acceptable to President Milosevic? There were no plans for unification because we did say that we had no designs on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. President Milosevic confirmed this because this plan is a plan for the future joint state of all the three nations living in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very rapidly and in a few more documents. First of all, as a matter of fact you've had a chance to review it and I don't need to go into it, Belgrade and Serbs generally were given the greatest possible warning of the views of the world as to what was happening in Bosnia by the interim decision, or however it was described, of the International Court of Justice on the 8th of April, 1993, wasn't it? You've had a chance to look at it. It's at tab 17. I'm not going to take the Court through it again.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because that report specified as an interim order prevention of genocide. What was the reaction of your leadership? You were there. What was the reaction of your leadership to such an extraordinarily grave interim order being made against you, to do nothing?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in 1993. It was within the competence of the Federal Ministry of Justice and the judiciary. This was a complaint that Muslim Bosnia sent to the International Court against Yugoslavia, naming Yugoslavia as an aggressor, and these were temporary measures issued by the ICJ which informed the federal organs. I don't know what was done further about this issue, but I know that this case is still pending before that court and has been for the past ten years or so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... cut across you. We've heard from Mr. Jovic. You know Mr. Jovic. He's explained to us in terms, both in his written statement and in his book, how the plan to develop the VRS as an army and the SPK army came from this accused because he recognised that leaving the JNA would expose Yugoslavia or the FRY to difficulties. Did he -- we've heard that. Did the accused not even raise the possibility of withdrawing support of funds from the Bosnian Serbs when an allegation of the kind made before the International Criminal -- Court of Justice was made?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These allegations were put forward by the Bosnian Muslim leadership and the court then issued a temporary measure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I must focus you on the question. We've heard --

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did the accused raise with his government the possibility of withdrawing funds from the Bosnian Serbs? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did this a year later, when very severe measures were introduced and relations broken off. In the meantime, he waged a Titanic struggle with them to get them to accept each of the plans of the Contact Group; the first, second, and then the third plan. He had a lot of problems in convincing them, and from time to time he told them that Yugoslavia would not be a hostage to their irrational policies, and he told them about the aid that was being provided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He carried on financing the offices, as we all know now, through the 30th and 40th personnel centres and carried on with the policy until he was arrested, of paying Mladic. Did he not even discuss stopping the crimes that were being committed, reported and reaching the level of interim orders about genocide from the International Court of Justice, did he not even discuss withdrawing funds?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that three-sided civil war, each side had its supporters, financially and otherwise, and they were all to a greater or lesser extent involved in a series of crimes. The fact that attention was being focused on the crimes of only one side and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... stop you there for a minute. Each side had its supporters, and you knew that you were supporting one side, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Politically, financially, and diplomatically, yes. They were our people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... militarily through finance, if nothing more.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know about that part because, as I told you, I knew nothing of military matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you know because you --

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- referred to crimes by all three sides. You knew that the side you were supporting was committing crimes.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We constantly condemned ethnic cleansing, the use of violence and the shelling of those towns, and we persistently demanded that they accept a cease-fire and even to declare a unilateral cease-fire. Our resistance to violence was continuous. We did not push Bosnia and Herzegovina into war. Those who pushed Bosnia and Herzegovina into war were those who would not accept Cutileiro's plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You and all of you working with this accused accepted the crimes that you knew were being committed and that you were funding, because you were working according to the accused's plan, that if you waited long enough, it would all fall in, by law or by negotiation, in the same way as it had fallen in by fighting and by killing in 1992; correct? And that's what this case is about, you see. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not correct. You have to take a broader view. Serbia received the largest number of refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina; about half a million. These people were not fleeing from something good. They were fleeing from something bad. The crimes that were committed were not just against Muslims, it was against the Serbs as well. We condemned all crimes and the forcible takeover of territory by all sides. We kept stressing that and we said that in our talks with the Serbs from Bosnia and Herzegovina. You cannot accuse us of supporting crime. We financially supported our people there, but we did not support crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I must move very rapidly, if I can. Can I just summarise the position to the witness because he's had a chance to look at some documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that you've been able to review, over the weekend, I hope, documents to which I will not be taking you, but the Security Council Resolution 819 of the 16th of April, 1993; the Resolution 820 of the 17th of April, 1993? Just yes or no, you've reviewed those?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Incidentally, the Council of Harmonisation records for the 20th of April, we've only been provided by the authorities with something called a minute, a short document. We have not been provided by the authorities with the long version of the document. Can you point us to -- they say that they -- the authorities say that they don't have it. Can you point us to where we might find such a full stenographically recorded version of what is only provided by a minute for that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What tab is that, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The tab is --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point us to where you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think you're addressing the wrong side, because I never had any of these documents at my disposal, and I have forgotten many things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have helped jog my memory. However, in the document you mention I cannot find anything worthy of special attention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's because you've only been provided with the minute. [B/C/S on English channel] Let me make it plain -- [B/C/S on English channel] We looked last week tabs 20 to 26, which covered Srebrenica and Sarajevo. We looked last week at tab 27, Resolution 819, at tab 28, which concerned Sarajevo, and then coming to 1995, we looked at tabs 30 to 34 which covered Tuzla, hostages, Sarajevo, and Srebrenica, to tab 35, Resolution 1004 which covered Srebrenica and hostages, to tabs 36 to 41 which covered Srebrenica and Zepa. Keeping your eye and mind on Zepa, can we look now at tab 42.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I would ask the remaining tabs, if the accused will consent, tabs 42 to 47, which are the same kind as the bulk of the exhibits we were looking at on the last occasion, tab 48 which is Resolution of the Security Council 1010, tabs 49 to 50, which are further communications of the same type, tab 51 which is a report, and then tabs 53, 54, and 57 which are further reports, might all be admitted as documents containing allegations and information. Ms. Dicklich reminds me that tab 48 is already in, but apart -- that's my application. Because otherwise I shall have to go through, however swiftly, the exercise with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, will you agree to those tabs going in?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not agree, Mr. Robinson, because I think that the tabs can go in if a witness is asked a question about the document and provides an answer. Otherwise, it's completely unacceptable. Otherwise, you can introduce as many things as you like into the record without anyone understanding what the documents are about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll see if Mr. Jovanovic will help us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, have you, over the weekend, had a chance to look at those tabs I've referred to, being severally communications of a certain type we dealt with last week and otherwise documents of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are well-known documents adopted by the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other documents, the documents that provided information to you, having reviewed them, are they indeed all documents that did provide information to you of the same kind that we were looking at last week?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the question is addressed to me --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I can confirm that these documents, up to the time I was there, which was mid-August 1995, were documents I knew about. The documents after that time are something I was not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, I shall have to deal with it. He says mid-1995, so these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: August --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's fine. In which case then we are all right, I think. Perhaps they can all go in, with Your Honours' leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us make it clear, we're talking about tabs 42, 43, 44, 45, 46, 47, 49, 50, 51 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, not 51.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not 50?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, 50 is one as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, those may be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the position is this, Mr. Jovanovic: In the period of time July and into August of 1995, you received repeated information from different locations expressing fear for Srebrenica, fear for Zepa; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There's a lot of that in the documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Zepa was saveable. Why didn't the accused or you or the government do anything to save Zepa once Srebrenica had fallen?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally had no ability to influence this, but Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had for a year had no contacts with the political leadership of Republika Srpska. Perhaps there was some lesser channels --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... then? If they had no contact with them, why did they still pay for their officers? It was your government. And people died as a result in large numbers of a funded army. Why did you not withdraw payment?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian army in Bosnia was also financed by the Republic of Croatia and nobody noticed anything. On the other hand, we kept drawing attention publicly to the fact that protected areas were not to be taken, not only Srebrenica and Zepa but others as well, Sarajevo and the others. That was our standpoint that we kept repeating. We constantly kept saying this should not be done. The facts indicate that the influence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the leadership in the Republika Srpska was not sufficient to prevent this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I just go back to the tabs while we're reasonably proximate to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The witness's answer was that the documents until the middle of August 1995 were documents he had been aware of. Tab 51 is dated the 30th of August, 1995; 53, 9th of November, 1995; 54, 27th of November, 1995; and 57 is the 21st of December, 1995. Was it the Bench's intention to rule that in although it was outside the parameters of the witness's answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I notice the witness said these are well-known documents adopted by the Security Council. Line 14, page 54.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I understand there are objections to postman, which we have had as an issue raised in the context of this witness's evidence, and I'm afraid that's exactly what the Bench would be doing with this witness as he is being used by the Prosecution. It would be the same issue, to the same effect, and that is my concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I make just one obvious point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He did say he was aware of them as well-known public documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It may be that he was aware of them, but what that goes to is a completely different matter. I think it needs some care looking at. He wasn't actually accepting them in his evidence, if one goes back into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I help, to save time? The witness was the representative of Yugoslavia in New York at the United Nations. If he's not aware of these documents, I have no idea who is supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's the same issue with the white book, though, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not really the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is a well-known document. The volumes of the white book is a well-known public document in Yugoslavia that he received and passed into the UN system. There is no difference here between what the Prosecution is trying to achieve and what the accused was attempting to achieve. Now, there should not be any greater credibility given to the documents of one party at the expense of the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So your submission is that all the documents dated after -- is it August 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, if there is to be consistency on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think the white book is a different matter. The accused was attempting to introduce it as evidence of the truth of those allegations of mistreatment and crimes, and we held that it could not be treated in that way at this time. We marked it for identity. We needed evidence as to how it was compiled. Here the witness is saying that he was aware of these as they were public documents. I mean, he was, after all, a senior figure in his government, working at the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He wasn't at the UN, though, for those particular tabs. Those are outside his stewardship. He was until mid-August 1995, and those four tabs I've pointed out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My understanding, Mr. Kay, is that he goes to the United Nations in 1995 until 2000, and what you've got is moving in mid-August from being a domestic minister to the United Nations where he then represented Serbia and -- the Republic of Yugoslavia at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would it be helpful if the foundation was set? The trouble is in doing things so quickly in such a large scale, one has to keep track of what is actually going in. I don't know if that commends itself to the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'll ask Mr. Nice to just lay a foundation for those last four tabs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, when did you arrive at the United Nations as the representative?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived there, if I remember well, on the 17th of September, 1995, or perhaps the 18th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The documents we've been looking at, we've been speaking about, are reports to the Secretary-General focused on Yugoslavia dated the 30th of August, the 2nd of November, the 9th of November, the 27th of November. I may have included one that's already in. Are those documents you had a duty to read in your capacity as the representative of your country?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I naturally did have that duty. However, that was after the fact. As I wasn't present at the mission of Yugoslavia in New York, I had to read it subsequently because it arrived on the 30th of August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just have a look, shall we, since the point is taken by my learned friend Mr. Kay, at tab 55. It was produced last time. And we'll lay on the overhead projector the first page in which the second line of the second paragraph -- next page, please. Sorry. The next page. Second line of the second paragraph reads: "In view of the shortcomings of the report of the Secretary-General of the 27th of November, 1995..." Now, we know you said last week that somebody else wrote this report for you, but you seem to have indicated that you've read the report. Had you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, I would like to reiterate that I challenged the claim that this document was sent Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to the right address. It was sent erroneously to the president of the Security Council. It was intended for the Russian representative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. Please. I would like to confirm this once again. Mr. Nice, last time you challenged my credibility, and you did it with an emphasis, and I would like to protest against that. I would like the Court to ask, through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, my associates to provide statements, namely Dragan Zupanjevac, Dragana Filipovic, and Petar Tasic [phoen]. These are my associates who can confirm that my instructions were not to send it to the president of the Security Council but to the head of the Russian mission, and afterwards everybody confirmed that they were precisely my instructions that were misunderstood by my deputy. Therefore, this should not be seen as a document reflecting my position or the position of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you going to repeat what you said last time, that you barely read it and that somebody else wrote it for you, or are you going to accept that this is your text?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, let me reiterate. As the session of the Security Council was to be held and it was to be devoted to Srebrenica, the head of the Russian mission asked us whether we had information. As I didn't have any information, I officially asked for the information. I was provided nothing. I pressed for it. And it wasn't until just prior to the beginning of the Security Council session that I received information from the Government of Republika Srpska. I personally did not agree with what was stated there. It didn't seem trustworthy. So I asked my deputy to go through it and to see whether there was anything there that could be sent to the head of the Russian mission. I was convinced it was sent to the Russian mission and not to the president of the Security Council. As I said, it was erroneously sent to the Security Council and I regret that deeply, and I would ask the Honourable Chamber to verify this with the people whose names I just gave to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I simply haven't the time to deal with much of what you're saying but let's just go to the point I was asking you to look at. "In view of the shortcomings of the report ... of the 27th of November 1995 and insufficient evidence on the alleged violations of humanitarian law and human rights, particularly with regard to the areas of Republika Srpska, we are very much concerned that members of the Security Council will not be in a position to fully ascertain the situation ..." Do you accept authorship or responsibility for those lines? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not accept --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, very well.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because this was written by my deputy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back to 54, then, and let's look at it since you insist on taking that line. 54 is the report referred to of the 27th of November, 1995. And we'll look at it on the overhead projector. And we'll put page 2 on. And we'll look at paragraph 5, Mr. Jovanovic. You're very concerned about whose -- who sent what and to whom, but now please look at paragraph 5. This report records "Thousands of people still remain unaccounted for." Paragraph 6 says, line three: "... a total of 8.000 tracing requests." Paragraph 7 says, "... ICRC has limited access to the prisoners." Paragraph 8 says, "Based on all the available information, it would appear that at least 3.000 but less than 8.000 people from Srebrenica are still missing." Well, we know that the RS has admitted to 7.000 deaths. Tell us, did you as representative of your country at the United Nations read this report dealing with, as we now know, 7.000 killings? Did you?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read this, naturally. However, I did not have confirmation that it had indeed been done to 7.000 people. I was shocked by the figure. But as I said before, things need to be confirmed from several sources.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... turns out to be true. Let's go back to your letter since - I beg your pardon, the letter you inadvertently signed, at tab 55, shall we. Can we put that on the overhead projector again. Don't let me beat about the bush,

utterances.speaker: MR. JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: You're trying to mislead this court and you're not telling the truth. You were prepared to pen --

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I protest. I apologise, Mr. Nice, but you have no right to call me a liar. I've sworn to tell the truth and what I'm saying is an absolute truth. I would ask the Court to verify this information with the persons whose name I gave to you and they will be able to confirm whether I'm telling the truth or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 3, please. Page 3, please. Let's just look at something. The end of this paragraph, on the very page where you put your signature, has Miroslav Deronjic. Now, you've heard of him, haven't you? Haven't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of him. I think that he was tried here or something like that. But prior to that, no, I never heard of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was informed that they did not find any substantial evidence to confirm the alleged crimes on mass graves. That was the sort of material you were relying on in your statement against the body of the detailed report by the United Nations. And if we go back through the pieces of information that I've dealt with very briefly, you'd already learnt about the aerial photographs produced at the United Nations by Madeleine Albright, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will say once again: The information that was erroneously sent to the Security Council was neither my position or the position of Yugoslav government. That was information provided by the Government of Republika Srpska, and it's stated very clearly at the very beginning of that unfortunate report. And let me reiterate once again: It was sent to that address erroneously. On the other hand, what was shown by Madam Albright I cannot comment on that. I wasn't present at the Security Council at the time but I have to admit that she was quite strict when it came to Bosnian Serbs and Serbs in general and that her words could not always be relied upon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is this the position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, just a minute. Since the witness has on two occasions asked the Court to verify what he has said today, it should be made clear that that is not a matter for the Court but for the accused.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Almost my last question, Mr. Jovanovic, is this, in light of your persisting in the answers you're giving: On this occasion the words of the RS were good enough for your government. Is that because the acts of the RS were the acts of your government?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a ludicrous conclusion. This document which was sent erroneously clearly indicates that that was information provided by the government of Republika Srpska. It doesn't state anywhere that it was provided by the government of Yugoslavia. So you cannot draw those conclusions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One last matter for detail that I ought to cover with this witness before he goes. In the course of your evidence, Mr. Jovanovic, you said in an exchange with this accused that a letter was -- on the 15th of February and in the version I've got it's page 25 and 26 of the then-transcript. You said of -- you were asked about a letter sent to Alija Izetbegovic, and you answered a question about that, and you said you informed Mr. Izetbegovic that you'd sent a similar letter to General Mladic with similar contents. So you were speaking of two letters sent by the accused to Mladic and Izetbegovic, and those letters were dated, you will remember, on or about the 1st of August of 1995. Now, I don't have a version that I can lay before you at the moment of those letters, but just confirm a couple of things for us. They were both in English, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. However, I didn't write them. Those letters were written by President Milosevic. Now, whether they were in English or in Serbian, I don't know. Why would they be in English? Maybe they were in English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Precisely. I'm going to suggest to you that perhaps you do know. But by the 1st of August, with the flow of information coming to this accused, he needed to set up a smokescreen of innocence and to detach himself from Mladic and from what had happened in Srebrenica, and that's why he wrote letters designed to present himself in a falsely favourable light in English. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is your conclusion. You keep trying to sell a claim that has no value. Mr. Milosevic already for a year had no contact with their political leadership. Therefore, he could not influence them and create a smokescreen. He had already condemned their policy and set up very strict border controls and invited international observers to monitor that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a blatant untruth. I did not send a letter to Mr. Izetbegovic in English, and I don't know how come Mr. Nice is putting that to the witness. Why would I be writing to Alija Izetbegovic in English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not a matter that you can take up in that way, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whether the original's in another language or not I can't say, but let me just make this point to you: You know, don't you, Mr. Jovanovic, that from the fall of Srebrenica right round and until 1996, despite the flow of information coming about Mladic, despite Mladic being indicted by this Tribunal, you and the accused met Mladic, you met him in meetings -- the accused met Mladic and there was no difficulty in contacting Mladic, was there?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, many other international mediators met with Mladic too. Therefore, that cannot be reduced to contacts only with him. As far as I remember, I met him only once during that period of time, and I did that because there were international visitors. Now, as to contacts with President Milosevic, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can point to no single condemnation of Mladic by this accused, no single querying of what Mladic had done, by this accused, throughout that period of time in which he was supported and in which time efforts were made to free him from ever being handed over to this Tribunal. Is that summary correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is your summary. This is how you wish to portray matters. I don't have such information. I wasn't informed about the developments enough in order to draw conclusions. I'm afraid that your conclusion is very tendentious.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. The four documents are admitted. Mr. Milosevic, re-examination. And remember, no leading questions. The four documents are tabs 51, 53, 54, and 57.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 55, I think, is one other outstanding number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was dealt with already. It was admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand that was already admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The cables. Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Re-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovanovic, as you spent several years at the UN as head of the Yugoslav mission, I assume that you are very familiar with the way that Security Council Resolutions are adopted.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at least those which pertain to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking about those which pertain to us. I'm interested in the procedure for adopting Resolutions. Do you know, first of all, that there is first a draft Resolution made, then there is a proposal made, which goes to the blue file and remains there for 24 hours, and then the Resolution is adopted?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the regular procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, each draft Resolution is placed in the white folder as a proposal and then, after 24 hours, is being voted upon by the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, unless it is amended in the meantime or replaced by another draft, which is exactly the reason why it is kept in the blue file.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the date of the Resolution is the date when it was voted on and adopted.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, let us compare two documents of the UN. One can be found in tab 8 of my binder, which is the report of the Secretary-General, and the other one can be found in tab 11 of Mr. Nice's binder, which is the Resolution of the Security Council containing the formulation of sanctions against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I hope that you have both documents before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: At tab 11 we don't have. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's an existing exhibit, therefore it was provided for convenience to the accused but for others it was not provided as a separate repeat document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can it be put on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course. I have a copy here that is highlighted. I think Ms. Dicklich has one that is not highlighted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Bear in mind that tab 11 is on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now please turn to page 3 of tab 11, which is Resolution 757, from 1992. 30th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us find it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please place the first page on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Therefore, can we all see that this is the Security Council Resolution which was adopted on the 30th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order for it to be adopted on the 30th of May, does it mean that, in accordance with the established procedure, it had to be submitted into the blue file at least on the 29th of May?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That would be in accordance with the procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, turn to page 3, please. Please take a look at page 3. There are several paragraphs. Item 1 in the middle of page 3 says: "[In English] Condemns the failure of the authorities in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, including the Yugoslav People's Army, to take effective measures to fulfil the requirements of Resolution 752." [Interpretation] Does the Resolution 752 pertain to withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army forces from Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, among other things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So the Security Council condemns the failure of the authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, including the JNA, to do so. Now, please take a look at tab 8, which was also quoted by Mr. Nice. This is the Secretary-General report. Now, let us first establish facts pertaining to dates. Please put tab 8 on the ELMO. Page 1, please. Can we see here that this is a report of the Secretary-General pursuant to paragraph 4 of Security Council Resolution 752, and can it be clearly seen that the date is the 30th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is the same date on which the Resolution was adopted, a Resolution that should have been placed in the blue binder the day before?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it an indisputable fact that this report was not considered before the adoption of the Resolution?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is more than evident because it arrived post festum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's look at the discrepancies and contradictions between this report and the Resolution. The Resolution states that the Security Council condemns the government of Yugoslavia and the JNA for not taking effective measures. In the report dated on the same day as the Resolution that was adopted, it says -- look at paragraph 6. "Most of these --" paragraph 6, second sentence -- can you hear me? My microphone is going on and off. We can read it all, but it says here: "[In English] Most of these are believed to have withdrawn already into Serbia and Montenegro, some of them having been subjected to attack during their withdrawal." [Interpretation] And then it goes on to say: "Others, however, remain at various garrisons in Bosnia-Herzegovina [In English] areas, including two installations on the outskirts of Sarajevo. A further category consists of personnel who have been blocked in their barracks by Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina or hostile irregular forces." [Interpretation] And then it goes on to explain where they are. Is it indisputable that this shows that the JNA forces did withdraw from Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is clearly stated. As long as it depended on them alone. They were unable to do so when they were prevented by the army of Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I must, I suppose, take some steps to stop questions that begin - this is the second one - is something indisputable. I don't think the answers are ever of any value if questions are formulated in that way. I beg your pardon. It may be the Chamber will decide that they are of no such value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Avoid that introductory phrase.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will avoid the introductory phrase, but I did not feel this to be a leading question because it points to the text of a document issued by the United Nations, a Resolution and a report by the Secretary-General. However, I will put my question differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, between what the Secretary-General's report dated the 30th of May, 1992, and what it says in the Security Council Resolution of the same date, which was adopted on the 30th of May, 1992, regarding the situation regarding the withdrawal of the army from Bosnia and Herzegovina, is there a contradiction?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There evidently is, because in paragraph 1, Yugoslavia is condemned for failing to comply with Resolution 752 and withdrawing the JNA, while here the opposite is stated, that Yugoslavia has done this. But in order for it to do this a hundred per cent, it could not do so because it was prevented by Alija Izetbegovic who blocked a barracks. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let us make a small digression in connection with the comparison between these two documents and my intention of showing that the Secretary-General's report was not taken into consideration when the Resolution was adopted. So I will quote paragraph 5 of the Secretary-General's report. Mr. Nice quoted only half of this paragraph, not all of it, when he put his question to you as to how the army of RSK was established. "[In English] The bulk of the JNA personnel --" [Interpretation] Is there a translation?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Repeat: "[In English] -- who were deployed in Bosnia and Herzegovina were citizens of that republic and were not therefore covered by the Belgrade authorities' decision of 4th of May to withdraw JNA from Bosnia and Herzegovina." [Interpretation] It goes on to describe what happened to them. "[In English] Most of them appear to have joined the army of the so-called 'Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina'. Others have joined the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is under the political control of the Presidency of that republic. Others may have joined various irregular forces operating there." [Interpretation] What does this tell us, Mr. Jovanovic, in order to avoid putting a leading question?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this explains that Yugoslavia -- or, rather, the JNA fulfilled the essence of its obligation from Resolution 752 and explains how this came about. All the soldiers and officers born in Montenegro and Serbia withdrew. Those who were born in and were citizens of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina remained and joined the so-called new army of the Republika Srpska or various territorial units. In any case, what happened here was what happened to the JNA from Slovenia onwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I just ask a question. Do you know what percentage, Mr. Jovanovic, of the JNA personnel deployed in Bosnia and Herzegovina were in fact citizens of that republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to this report, 80 per cent of the JNA personnel were citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, while 20 per cent were citizens of Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I go on, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of these 80 per cent who were citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in paragraph 5 it says that they -- let me be precise: "[In English] The bulk of the JNA personnel who were deployed in Bosnia and Herzegovina were citizens of that republic ..." [Interpretation] And then it goes on to say: "[In English] ... and were not therefore covered by Belgrade authorities' decision." [Interpretation] It goes on: "Most of them appear to have joined the army of the so-called 'Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina.'" This is part of that 80 per cent. They joined the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And the next sentence goes on to say: "Others have joined the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is under the political control of the Presidency of that republic." The majority of the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina making up the JNA in Bosnia and Herzegovina separated into those who joined the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and those who joined the army under the control of Alija Izetbegovic. Is that what it says here?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those soldiers who were of Muslim ethnicity or, rather, the Islamic religion, of course didn't want to stay in the army of Republika Srpska. They joined the other side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going into what is natural or not, just into the facts in this report. Let us now return to paragraph 1 of the Secretary-General's report in order to establish how things happened. It says here in paragraph 2, where it says "Background": "[In English] On 26 April 1992, President Izetbegovic of Bosnia and Herzegovina met at Skopje with General Blagoje Adzic, Chief of Staff of JNA and Acting Federal Secretary for Defence, and Mr. Branko Kostic, vice-president of the Federal Presidency in Belgrade, to define the role of JNA in Bosnia and Herzegovina and its overall withdrawal."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's "eventual withdrawal."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. "And its eventual withdrawal." Yes, Mr. Robinson, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "[In English] This meeting did not produce a definitive agreement, and the Belgrade authorities on 4 May announced their decision to withdraw from Bosnia-Herzegovina by 18 May all JNA personnel who were not citizens of that republic. On 13 May, Vice-president Kostic proposed to President Izetbegovic that the talks be resumed with the participation of representatives of the Bosnian Serb and Croat communities. On the same day, authorities of the so-called 'Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina' announced their decision to form their own army, which would be composed of units of the former JNA based in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and appointed General Ratko Mladic as Commander of that army." [Interpretation] Are you aware that the vice-president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, and this was the Supreme Command of the armed forces, the vice-president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia and the chief of the General Staff and the acting minister of defence met with Izetbegovic in Skopje and attempted to solve the problems of the JNA in Bosnia and Herzegovina? There was no agreement, as can be seen here, and the Presidency reached the decision that the JNA personnel who did not originate from Bosnia and Herzegovina be withdrawn. Are you aware that -- are you aware of what the deputy president, Mr. Kostic, proposed to Alija Izetbegovic, asking him to call upon the Serbian and Croatian communities to take over the personnel and equipment of the JNA belonging to them remaining in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Do you know more about this?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know only about the existence of such a proposal, "that this issue should be resolved in agreement with all interested parties and that the JNA should withdraw, in agreement with the wishes and will of everyone, of all concerned." As we can see from this text, this was not accepted. After this, the federal leadership reached a decision to withdraw all the units of the JNA with a deadline of the 19th of May, if I remember correctly. Those who were citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina had the option of remaining in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and most of them did so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The president of the Presidency proposed to Alija Izetbegovic that all three ethnic communities should take over the property and personnel of the JNA on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is this what happened?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the essence of his proposal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, look at paragraph 2. "On 17 May I received a letter --" this means the Secretary-General received a letter "-- from Admiral Miroslav Simic, [In English] Chief of General Staff JNA, requesting --" [Interpretation] It's quite unclear here. I think it says assistance -- "[In English] in the safe withdrawal of JNA troops from Bosnia and Herzegovina, and particularly from Sarajevo, Pazaric and Zenica. The letter referred inter alia to an agreement, to an agreement signed on 10th of May at the premises of United Nations Protection Forces in Yugoslavia, (UNPROFOR), at Sarajevo by representatives of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, JNA, the European Community Monitoring Mission, and the personal envoy of Lord Carrington, Mr. Colm Doyle. On 21st of May, vice-president Kostic again wrote to ask me to request President Izetbegovic to order the deblocking of the JNA garrison at Sarajevo. On 25 May 1992, I received a letter from President Izetbegovic in which, inter alia, he requested that UNPROFOR should supervise the withdrawal of part of the JNA personnel and weapons, in accordance with the agreement of 10 May..." [Interpretation] Are you aware, Mr. Jovanovic, of what happened in Dobrovoljacka street when the JNA column was attacked which was being escorted by UNPROFOR? UNPROFOR was overseeing the withdrawal leading the convoy, it was there on the spot, and do you remember the massacre of that convoy?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I repeat what I have said on many occasions: It doesn't concern me how the accused uses his time, but I wonder whether the Chamber would want to consider whether what's now being engaged in really arises out of cross-examination by doing a long textual analysis of the document again, only asked a few questions, partly for want of time and partly for other reasons, and we're now taking something out of the document and going to the underlying facts of it. It's a matter for the Chamber, but it doesn't seem to me necessarily to be re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but I think you did raise issues relating to this report, Mr. Nice, and I think the accused is entitled to re-examine on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Matter for the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In any case, let us be brief. The main element in the report, where it says that the JNA withdrew from Bosnia and Herzegovina, when this is compared with the Resolution bearing the same date, the 30th of May, 1992, points to major discrepancies between the contents of the Resolution and the contents of the report. To whose detriment are these discrepancies?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Evidently to the detriment of Yugoslavia. As for the text you read out, I wish to mention General MacKenzie's book where he describes in detail how this all came about and who was responsible for the death of these cadets in Dobrovoljacka street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will not quote again paragraph 6 from the Secretary-General's report which says they did withdraw and were exposed to attacks during withdrawal. Let us, rather, go to the Resolution in tab 11 and paragraph 2. In paragraph 1, the Serbs are condemned for something that was not actually true, and paragraph 2 demands that any element of the Croatian army still present in Bosnia and Herzegovina act in accordance with paragraph 4 of Resolution 752 without further delay. Would you now please look here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you're going to try to finish now, because we are at the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will just round off this topic, and it will take me a minute and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 10 of the Secretary-General's report, it says: "[In English] As regards the element of withdrawal of the Croatian army now in Bosnia-Herzegovina, information currently available in New York suggests that no such withdrawal has occurred. UNPROFOR has received reliable reports of Croatian army personnel in uniform operating within, and as part of, military formations in Bosnia and Herzegovina..." [Interpretation] and so on and so forth. What it says here in the Secretary-General's report in connection with the presence of the regular Croatian army in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as UNPROFOR reported, does it contradict paragraph 2 of the Resolution which says that any element of Croatian army still present?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this report, the Resolution should have been passed against Croatia, not us. I wish to remind Their Honours that a week before the adoption of this Resolution, the political director, Mr. Kirsay [phoen] said that the general perception was that it was our fault and this would remain, even though it was the Croatian army that was in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it was the perception that was important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jovanovic. I will not dwell further on this Resolution of the 30th of May and the Secretary-General's report of the 30th of May. I believe that this is now sufficiently clear and that the links between those two documents which are evidently non-existent have been demonstrated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One question. Mr. Jovanovic, if you take a look at paragraph 17 of the Secretary-General's report, while we are on that document, that reads: "The Security Council's decision today to impose sanctions on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia creates a new situation. It is not yet clear what implications this will have for the issues discussed in this report." Did the Secretary-General not envisage that there will be a Security Council Resolution on the very same day, imposing sanctions on Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say what the Secretary-General thought, whether he envisaged it or not, but if he was familiar with the report which he signed, and he had to be familiar with it before the 30th, then he could not, at least intimately, have agreed with the text of the Resolution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, the question put to you by Mr. Kwon only goes to confirm that the report was drawn up on the day when the Security Council was sitting and reaching a decision on sanctions. What does this mean? This Security Council Resolution today creates a new situation. "[In English] It is not yet clear what implications this will have for the issues discussed in this report." Does it seem to you that the Secretary-General warned --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Seems like a leading questioning coming, to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Rephrase, Mr. Milosevic. After the break. I think we should take the break now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, let us briefly return to the Security Council Resolution dated the 30th of May, which we can find in tab 11, where in the introductory part, as is usual, they refer to the Secretary-General's report. Please take a look at page 2 of this Resolution, where somewhere towards the bottom -- or, rather, the fourth paragraph from the bottom, "expressing its appreciation for the report of Secretary-General of the 26th of May, 1992 Resolution 752." What is stated here, does it point to the fact that this Resolution refers to the report of 26th of May and that the 30th of May report is not being mentioned anywhere?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, to go back to the question raised by Mr. Kwon about Secretary-General saying that what the Security Council is deciding upon today about the sanction creates the situation that this is not yet clear what implications this will have for the issues discussed in this report. Is this some kind of a warning or reservation expressed or it has no significance at all?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is both a kind of reservation and a warning, because there are always uncertainties and dangers that can follow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I was unable to find the Secretary-General's report dated the 26th. However, I will look for it, Mr. Robinson, because it is obvious that it differs quite a lot from the report of the 30th. Yes. This report came four days after the report mentioned in the Resolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice raised the issues contained in tab 15, which are stenograms from the extended session of the coordination council. Please take a look at the page where stenogram starts. This is not really in chronological order because page 2 comes before page 1, but the title is Stenographic Notes from the Extended Session of the Council. Does it stem from the first paragraph, which lists those in attendance, that towards the end, when all the officials of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Republic of Serbia and Montenegro are mentioned, at the end it states: "Members of the council," which is the ninth line from the top. Those attending, the Academician Dobrica Cosic, president of Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, president of the council; Radoje Kontic, vice-president of the government; Momir Bulatovic, and so on, Dr. Svetozar Stojanovic, special advisor to the president of the Serbia is the last name, and then it says members of the council, and then they proceed to enumerate persons which in the translation that can be seen on the ELMO shows that it was done in a different form. The names are listed differently than in the original, because first they list members of the council and then the persons attending the session. Can you see that in the stenographic notes before you?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that in the Serbian version and also in the other one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please put page 1 of the Serbian version on the ELMO so that we can see just to what extent it differs from the translation. The translation, in fact, does not distinguish between the members of the council and those who, according to the person chairing the session, invite -- were invited. Please take a look at the stenographic notes in their original version. So after that, in line nine from the top, after they list those attending, including the advisor, they proceed to say: "Member of the council," and then there's a colon and the names, Colonel General Zivota Panic, and so on, the other names. Mr. Jovanovic, was this council a forum for exchange of opinions or was it an organ that was able to pass decisions?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was mostly the former. It was a forum where positions were coordinated and opinions adopted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose positions were coordinated or harmonised? Because we can see that the top officials of Yugoslavia and the republics attended this session. So whose positions were harmonised?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The positions of representatives of these two Serb republics, because all of this has to do with Vance-Owen Plan. These issues had to be dealt with in such a way as to make the plan acceptable for them as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, does the Serbian document indicate the two categories that Mr. Milosevic was identifying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because in the Serbian document, on page 10, after enumerating members of the council, there's a dash and then members of the council follows. So this clearly distinguishes between the two categories. So it is quite clear who are the members of the council and who are the invited guests.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, please tell us at whose initiative these people were invited to attend the sessions of the council. Was it the chairman of the council, or whose initiative was it? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was at the initiative of the president of the council, Dobrica Cosic. I received notice to attend from his cabinet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it mean that everybody who was invited to the session was expected to present their views?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was expected. If they were invited, then it was assumed that they would present their views about the difficulties, how to resolve them, the process, and so on; otherwise, what would be the point of inviting them?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, please go to page 34, because Mr. Nice quoted several things mentioned earlier by me -- rather, quoted my words. On page 34 it says: "Slobodan Milosevic." In the middle of third paragraph. Before that I say: "I would propose that we look at what is on the table and what we should do right now." And then I say: "First of all, I would not like to go into a scholastic discussion about small and major steps. I would rather speak about good and bad steps. A major bad step is definitely worse than a small bad step." And then in the next paragraph, I say: "Our strategic goal is to ensure that the Serb people in the Balkans are free and equal -- have equal rights with others." Is that what it states, Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this is the main point of your position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then towards the end I say: "It is less important to me through how many institutional phases we need to go. What is more important is how many people will have to die for those goals and should -- should somebody die." Is that what it says here?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, I have to say that this was also contained in the letters sent by you to the leadership of Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina when they refused to accept certain peace plans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, please go to page 38, passage in the centre of the page. Still I am the one speaking. "Therefore, I opt for a pragmatic approach to existing circumstances and situations and using all available possibilities in order to go further, then opting for confrontation, because that could lead to major bloodshed or could take us to a dead alley. We have to take a number of steps. However, we have to ensure that there is additional initiative for further peace negotiations. I think that this problem needs to be viewed from several aspects in order to find a good attitude or good solution for the further work of the conference." Is this the conference on former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I think the one held in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Milosevic please repeat what he read out. He's reading at quite a fast pace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the interpreters are asking you to repeat what you just read out, and they say you are moving too quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I will read slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once again I speak of the goal, and then it says: "The goal which has to do with freedom and equality of Serb people in the Balkan Peninsula. However, we need to ask ourselves through which institutional phases will the achievement of these goals have to pass." And then further on, on page 39: "Therefore, I suggest that we should consider that possible direction and review what steps are possible." Nikola Koljevic says: "Asking for a signature on the paper." Milosevic: "Why wouldn't we sign something that suits us if we are able to improve it?" Nikola Koljevic: "And if we're not able to improve it?" Milosevic: "There is no Atasari's constitution." If you remember, Atasari was Lord Owen's assistant. "You will be writing a constitution together with Alija and Boban." Alija Izetbegovic, the reference is made to him, and Mate Boban, president of the Croatian Community. Are these the people referred to?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then on page 40, Milosevic once again: "They are -- they have changed the principles in the discussions already. The one change is that they say three constituent people." He used the term "three constituent peoples." Is that what is stated here?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, this took place on the 9th of January, 1993. What actually took place at this meeting where everybody expressed their attitude as to how we should deal with the negotiations? What were we trying to do?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we were trying to do is convince representatives of Republika Srpska and Republic of Serbian Krajina that the most important thing was to ensure their freedom and equality and their constituent status and that to ensure that their vote is taken into account when deciding things in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were very agitated, they were very frustrated. They did not act logically. They were afraid that they would be manipulated and left without anything in the end. Therefore, your efforts to convince them, as well as efforts of President Cosic and myself, were aimed at that, to convince them that they had nothing to fear if they were granted everything that was stated in Vance-Owen Plan, and that plan offered a compromise for all three sides. And there was nothing there to indicate that there was an intention to grab the territories of Bosnia and Herzegovina or perhaps create Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Jovanovic, let us turn to tab 16, which is again a session of this council held on the 21st of January, 1993. So the topic is practically the same. Is that obvious to you as well, Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was on the 9th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And the next session was held on the 21st of January. So after 12 days. Please take a look at page 39. On page 39, it says: "Slobodan Milosevic," and then a colon and I will quote from the beginning, what is stated here: "I propose that we try and see what can be expected in Geneva. We have a position of a principled participant committed to a peaceful resolution of the crisis. We invested maximum efforts to ensure that a principled position is defined."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If he does want us to follow it, we don't have it yet on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's get it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 39.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I have notes dated January 9 here but we've already covered that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. We have covered that and now we have turned to tab 16.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then we have tab 16, from the session of the same council.

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, you say tab 16. Okay. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is that a session of the same council but held on the 21st of January?

utterances.speaker: VLADISLAV JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please put page 39 on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We haven't yet found the equivalent of page 39. I'm just looking for it at the moment. This is, I think, one of those versions which -- where the interpreters, when they did their work, didn't place the parallel page numbers. 34. Ms. Dicklich has found it. Page 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, please put page 39 on the ELMO, of the Serbian text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You want the Serbian text on the ELMO, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that is logical, because both of us speak Serbian, and you have the English text in front of you, and you can follow whether the interpreters are interpreting correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The problem is we don't have the English text. We are relying on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. All right. Then the interpreters will interpret it for you, I assume. I have what I received from Mr. Nice for his cross. This is not my exhibit. May I read out this quotation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
